sections.h2: How much does selling a house in New York change from place to place?
sections.html:
A great deal. The state has 20,002,427 residents, but the housing picture in New York City looks nothing like the one in a Westchester suburb, and the paperwork changes with it. The Census Bureau's state QuickFacts and its city profiles show the spread.

In the city, most households rent, which means a seller often deals with a building rather than a single house. In New Rochelle, a bit over half the homes are owner-occupied. Property tax rules, appeal dates and who collects the bill all depend on which of these worlds you sell in, and so does the type of buyer who will be interested in the property.

sections.h2: What taxes are due when a New York house is sold?
sections.html:
The state taxes the transfer itself. New York charges $2 for each $500 of consideration on any conveyance above $500, and the Tax Department's transfer tax page says that base tax falls on the seller unless the contract shifts it. The buyer owes the extra 1 percent mansion tax on a residence selling for $1 million or more.

  • Filing outside the city: Form TP-584 goes to the county clerk, with payment due within 15 days after the deed is delivered.
  • Filing inside the city: Form TP-584-NYC is used for every conveyance, and added city taxes begin at $2 million for residential sales.
  • Nonresident sellers: they compute gain on the sale and may owe estimated personal income tax unless an exemption on the form applies.
  • Company sellers or buyers: for a building with up to four dwelling units, the filing needs documents naming every member, manager and authorized person of an LLC.
  • Deeds from an inheritance: a conveyance by devise, bequest or inheritance is not a taxable conveyance.

sections.h2: Why do property tax bills work differently in each New York city?
sections.html:
Assessing is local. A town or city assessor values the property, and then separate taxing bodies set what they need from the roll, which is why the assessor cannot change your rate. The state Tax Department explains that review has two tiers, a local grievance first and then court review, either Small Claims Assessment Review or a tax certiorari case in State Supreme Court.

Grievance Day is typically the fourth Tuesday in May, though the state says to confirm the date with your assessor, and two places in this guide show how far the calendar can move:

  • New Rochelle takes complaints from February 1 through the third Tuesday of February, and it has not done a citywide revaluation since 1956.
  • New York City sends valuation notices in January, and the Tax Commission deadlines are March 15 for Class 1 and March 1 for the other classes.
  • New Rochelle collects for the city, county, school district and library in four payments, while New York City runs one Department of Finance bill on a July to June year.

Our local property tax guides for those two places go into dates, offices and unpaid tax in more detail. Elsewhere, ask your own assessor's office for the roll and the local calendar.

sections.h2: What is STAR and how does selling affect it?
sections.html:
STAR is the School Tax Relief program, and a homeowner who applies today registers with the state to receive a credit by check or direct deposit. The Tax Department says you register once and the credit is issued each year while you remain eligible.

A sale ends that arrangement for you. The state asks that you close your registration if you sell, and the buyer registers as soon as the home becomes a primary residence. Owners whose registration changes because of marriage, divorce, a trust or a survivorship transfer should update it. Anyone paying school tax through a mortgage escrow account should tell the lender when they switch from the exemption to the credit.

sections.h2: What does New York law say about foreclosure for a homeowner who wants to sell?
sections.html:
A lender has to give at least 90 days' notice before starting a foreclosure suit, which gives a homeowner time to weigh options such as a sale. The Department of Financial Services' Foreclosure Bill of Rights summarizes the steps under RPAPL sections 1303 and 1304.

  • You keep the right to live in the home and the duty to maintain it until a court orders otherwise.
  • You can stop a foreclosure by paying the loan in full before the sale or by reaching a settlement.
  • After you are served, an answer is due within 20 days if served personally and 30 days if served another way.
  • A mandatory settlement conference follows, where both sides must negotiate in good faith.
  • If the home resells for more than the debt, you can apply to the court for the surplus.

The notice a plaintiff must serve under section 1303 has to tell the homeowner about the right to stay until a foreclosure sale, along with the duty to keep the property in repair and to keep paying taxes. Abandoning the house can open the door to an expedited process, so the department urges owners to stay and answer every paper they receive.

Free help is available through the Homeowner Protection Program hotline at (855) 466-3456 and through nonprofit housing counselors listed by county on the department's website.

sections.h2: Who handles a house that came through an estate?
sections.html:
Probate cases belong to the Surrogate's Court. The New York courts site describes it as the court that hears matters about the affairs of decedents, including the probate of wills and the administration of estates, and notes that mediation is available as an alternative to litigation. New York City has its own Surrogate's Court page.

Deeds that pass through inheritance are outside the transfer tax, but a later sale by the heirs is a fresh conveyance with its own filing. If you inherited a house and want to sell, ask the Surrogate's Court clerk for the county where the person lived which papers a buyer's title company will need.

sections.h2: What happens to tenants when a New York landlord sells?
sections.html:
The tenant's deposit follows the building. General Obligations Law section 7-108 makes the buyer liable for a deposit it knew about, and a buyer is treated as knowing about deposits held in a bank during the six months before closing or noted in a lease in force at closing. When there is no record, the buyer must tell the tenant in writing within 30 days after closing.

Deposits are capped at one month's rent in most dwellings, and the landlord must return the balance with an itemized statement within 14 days after the tenant leaves. A seller with tenants in place should hand over the leases and deposit records at closing.

faqs.q: Who pays New York's real estate transfer tax?
faqs.a: The seller pays the base tax of $2 per $500 of price, unless the contract says otherwise. If the seller does not pay, the buyer must. The buyer pays the 1 percent mansion tax on residences of $1 million or more.

faqs.q: When is the transfer tax form due?
faqs.a: Within 15 days after the deed is delivered. Outside New York City the TP-584 goes to the county clerk, and in the city the TP-584-NYC is used.

faqs.q: How long do I have to respond to a New York foreclosure suit?
faqs.a: Twenty days if you were served in person and 30 days if served another way. Missing the deadline can cost you the chance to state your defenses.

faqs.q: Is Grievance Day the same everywhere in New York?
faqs.a: No. The state's usual date is the fourth Tuesday in May, but New Rochelle uses the third Tuesday in February and New York City works with March Tax Commission deadlines. Confirm the date with your assessor.

faqs.q: Do I still need to close my STAR registration if I sell?
faqs.a: Yes. The Tax Department says to close the registration when you sell, and the new owner registers separately.
